Catalyst-Controlled Formal [4+1] Annulation of N-Vinyl 
Fluorenone Nitrones and Allenoates to Prepare 
Spirofluorenylpyrrolines 
Cui Wei, Jin-Qi Zhang, Jia-Jie Zhang, Cui Liang, and Dong-Liang Mo*
We report a readily commercial Gimeracil-catalyzed formal [4+1] annulation approach for the synthesis of 
spirofluorenylpyrrolines in good yields with high diastereoselectivity from easily available N-vinyl fluorenone nitrones and 
allenoates. The reaction showed broad substrate scope and tolerated a variety of functional groups on both N-vinyl 
fluorenone nitrones and allenoates. Mechanistic studies showed that the catalyst might play important roles on promoting 
enolation and selective cyclization of 1,3-dicarbonyl intermediates. More importantly, the obtained 
spirofluorenylpyrrolines were easily converted to various spirofluorenylpyrroline-based scaffolds.
Introduction
The spirocyclic compounds are currently of great interest 
because 3D structures of spirocyclic scaffolds play important 
roles on the biological and pharmacological activities.1 The 
construction of spirocyclic scaffolds has long been considered 
significant but is a highly challenging task owing to its inherent 
conformational rigidity and steric hindrance.2,3 Therefore, 
development of new methods toward the preparation of 
spirocyclic compounds is desirable. Cycloaddition reaction, 
among the most efficient annulations to build heterocycles, 
has been successfully used to construct spirocyclic 
compounds.4 Nitrones have been extensively used as 1,3-
dipolar compounds in cycloaddition reactions to construct N, 
O-heterocycles since its discovery, which can not only 
participate in [3+2], [3+3], [4+3] or other relative 
cycloadditions, but also be used as O-sources in the O-transfer 
reaction.5,6 The [3+2] cycloaddition of nitrones with allenoates 
was reported before but it was always used to prepare 2,3-
disubstituted indoles or related benzoazepine scaffords 
(Scheme 1-A).7,8 In 2019, Prathapan and coworkers, developed 
a catalyst-free synthesis of 1-azaspiro[4.4]nonane-3-one 
through a [3+2] cycloaddition and sequential [1,3]-
rearrangement of 9-fluorenone nitrones and  1,1-disubstitued 
allenes, however, the substrate scope was limited (Scheme 1-
B).9 Recently, N-vinyl nitrones have been used as useful 
organic building blocks because the double bond of nitrone N-
atom can participate in many transformations to biuld 
complex targets.10 However, the cycloaddition of N-vinyl 
nitrones with allenoates was only one example reported up to 
now. In 2014, Anderson and co-workers found that N-vinyl 
fluorenone nitrones reacting with electron-deficient allenes 
and sequential [3,3]-rearrangement afforded various 1,4-
enamino ketones under catalyst-free conditions, which then 
underwent hydrolysis and condensation to result in pyrrole 
target (Scheme 1-C).11 They proposed a simple 1,4-addition 
reaction mechanism rather than undergoing [3+2] 
cycloaddition due to the sterically hindered and electronically 
deactivated fluorenyl imine group. These afforementioned 
reactions have showed their efficiency of nitrones to prepare 
indole or pyrrole heterocycles under the mild reaction 
coniditions, but they usually focused on a [3+2] annulation 
and the allenes served as 2C-or 3C-synthons. On the other 
hand, these reported examples have showed that the O-atom 
of nitrones was usually not transferred to the target products 
and ketones were always produced as waste after the reaction 
completed. Moreover, spirocyclic compounds containing 
fluorenyl groups usually possessed distinct properties owing 
to their high rigidity and steric hindrance.12 Therefore, the 
development of atom economic strategies to construct 
spirocyclic compounds containing fluorenyl groups is also 
valuable.
Recently, we have successfully developed [3+2] 
cycloaddition of 9-fluorenone nitrones with 
methylenecyclopropanes to afford various 
spirofluorenyl-β-lactams and spiropiperidin-4-ones, and [3+3] 
cycloaddition with aza-oxyallyl cations to afford 
spirofluorenyl-1,2,4-oxadiazinan-5-ones.13 During our studies 
on the applications of N-vinyl nitrones,14 compared to 
Anderson’s proposed mechanism,11 we supposed that a 
hydrogen-bonding catalyst might promote the 1,4-nucleophilic 
addition of N-vinyl fluorenone nitrones to allenoates and

Results and Discussion
Initially, N-vinyl fluorenone nitrone 1a and allenoate 2a 
were chosen as model substrates to test the effect of catalyst 
on the formal [4+1] annulation. As shown in Table 1, when 1a 
was reacted with 2a without catalyst in DCE at 40 °C, desired 
spirofluorenylpyrroline 3aa was not observed (Table 1, entry 
1). Pleasingly, 20% yield of 3aa was obtained when 20 mol% of 
Gimeracil (C1) was added to the reaction mixture (Table 1, 
entry 2). It is worthy to note that adding Gimeracil catalyst 
obviously shortened the reaction time to 12 h compared to 
Anderson’s work10 with 18-24 h, suggesting that Gimeracil 
could accelerate the reaction. Increasing the reaction 
temperature to 80 °C improved the yield of 3aa to 48% but 
decreased to 12% at 100 °C (Table 1, entries 3-4). We 
surmised that the hydrogen-bonding catalysts might promote 
the reaction, and then, phosphine catalyst C2 and thiourea 
catalysts C3-C4 were also tested. We found that C2 catalyst 
inhibited the reaction while C3 catalyst afforded 3aa in 34% 
yield (Table 1, entries 5-6). Adding chiral thiourea C4 furnished 
3aa in 31% yield without enantioselectivity (Table 1, entry 7). 
The ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) was also tested as catalyst 
and found that 3aa was afforded only in 8% yield (Table 1, 
entry 8). Solvent screening revealed that lower yields of 3aa 
were obtained in toluene, CHCl3, C6F6, and MeCN (Table 1, 
entries 9-12). We are pleased to find that DMF as solvent 
delivered 3aa in 66% yield (Table 1, entry 13). Decreasing the 
amount of Gimeracil to 10 mol% afforded 3aa in 51% yield 
(Table 1, entry 14). Increasing the amount of Gimeracil to 30 
mol% improved the yield of 3aa to 69% and further to 77% by 
adding 50 mol% of Gimeracil (Table 1, entries 15-16). 
Therefore, the optimal conditions for preparing 
spirofluorenylpyrroline 3aa was Gimeracil (50 mol%) in DMF at 
80 °C for 3 h.15

Next, various allenoates 2 were evaluated to determine 
their effect on the preparation of spirofluorenylpyrrolines. As 
shown in Table 3, all the allenoates 2b-2n were reacted with 
nitrone 1a smoothly to afford the corresponding products 
3ab-3an in moderate to good yields with trans diastereomers 
only. However, when t-Bu substituted allenoate 2f was carried 
out under the optimized conditions, compound 3af was not 
observed perhaps due to the large steric hindrance of 
allenoate. The allenoates tolerated various electron-
withdrawing groups (EWG), such as ester, ketone, and amides, 
delivering the corresponding spirofluorenylpyrrolines in good 
yields. It is worthy to note that compound 3aj was obtained as 
a mixture of enol and ketone with a 5.6:1 ratio owing to the 
existing enolation of 1,3-diketone group. The structure of 
compound 3 was determined by X-ray diffraction analysis of 
3ab.16 When reaction with (-)-menthol-derived allenoate 2m 
was carried out under the optimized conditions, product 3am 
was obtained in 48% yield with a 1:1 diastereoselectivity, 
showing that the auxiliary group of allenoates cannot control 
the diastereoselectivity of the pyrroline ring. Interestingly, 
methyl disubstituted allenoate 2n was subjected to the 
optimized conditions affording product 3an containing an all 
quaternary carbon center in 38% yield with a 20:1 dr. The 
relative configuration of 3an was determined by its NOESY 
spectrum, showing that the two methyl groups were in the 
same face.

Scheme 2. Mechanistic studies
Based on the above experimental results, a plausible 
mechanism for the formation of spirofluorenylpyrrolines 3 
from N-vinyl fluorenone nitrones 1 and allenoates 2 is 
illustrated in Scheme 3. The initial 1,4-nucleophilic addition of 
nitrone 1 and allenoate 2 under Gimeracil catalyst affords 
intermediate A,17 which undergoes [3,3]-rearrangement to 
result in intermediate B. The dicarbonyl groups of 
Intermediate B go through a selective enolation under the 
acidic C1-catalyst to furnish four-substituted enol 
intermediate C. Isomerisation of B delivers compound 5. Also, 
intermediate C isomerizes to intermediate D which exists a 
balance with intermediate C under the C1 catalyst. Finally, 
kinetically controlled intramolecular cyclization of 
intermediate C from the opposite face with R2 group provides 
product 3 and releases C1 catalyst. Under our optimized 
conditions, we does not observe compound 5, suggesting that 
C1 catalyst might play the roles of acidity and hydrogen-
bonding, which accelerate the reaction rate and facilitate the 
conversion of intermediate B to intermediate C instead of 
isomerisation to compound 5. The balance between C and D 
was supported by the experimental results of Scheme 2-2.

Scheme 3. Proposed mechanism
To demonstrate the advantages of this formal [4+1] 
annulation strategy, a gram scale performance of nitrone 1a 
was carried out under the optimal conditions (Scheme 4-1). 
When 1.0 g of N-vinyl fluorenone nitrone 1a was reacted with 
2a, product 3aa was obtained in 65% yield (0.89 g). Then, the 
transformations of 3aa were investigated (Scheme 4-2). 
Treating 3aa with NaBH4 in MeOH at room temperature 
afforded amino alcohol 6 in 61% yield with only one 
diastereomer, showing that the ketone, ester and imine 
groups were all reduced. Compound 3aa reacting with 
cyclopropenone under DBU in Et2O delivered 
spirofluorenylpyrrole-tethered -lactone 7 in 55% yield with a 
1.8:1 dr. Reaction of 3aa with benzene-1,2-diamine afforded 
compound 8 in 35% yield. These easy transformations expand 
the applications in the diversity of spirofluorenyl compounds 
and will allow more potent biological activity studies.

Conclusions
We have developed a metal-free atom economic strategy 
through a simple Gimeracil-controlled formal [4+1] annulation 
of N-vinyl fluorenone nitrones with allenoates. This reaction 
tolerates a broad range of N-vinyl fluorenone nitrones and 
allenoates to furnish various densely functionalized 
spirofluorenylpyrrolines. The present method features allenes 
as 1C-synthon and Gimeracil as a catalyst to achieve an atom 
economy reaction to afford spirocyclic compounds. More 
importantly, we have devised a novel platform for the N-vinyl 
fluorenone nitrones with allenoates, and it will provide a 
further design for other dipolarophiles into new reaction 
mode.
